spot: Four sailors were rescued alive in the remote South Pacific after their 52-foot yacht, Tai Tam, was sunk by a sperm whale. The crew endured an 18-hour ordeal, activating an emergency beacon after the collision 250 nautical miles north of Norfolk Island, before being transferred to a life raft and rescued by New Zealand military forces.
content_html:
Key Developments

A harrowing ordeal unfolded for four sailors aboard the 52-foot yacht Tai Tam when a pod of sperm whales struck their vessel in the remote South Pacific. The incident occurred 250 nautical miles north of tiny Norfolk Island, leading to the yacht's sinking and an 18-hour fight for survival on the high seas.

Australian crew member Jemma Cooper described a "loud thud" that pushed the entire boat sideways, throwing her from the steering wheel. She quickly noticed a brown discoloration in the water and a pod of six to eight sperm whales, confirming the cause of the impact. Her husband, Jeremy Cooper, sleeping below deck, was awakened by the collision and immediately recognized the severity of the situation, noting smashed steering gear and significant water ingress on the starboard side.

Approximately 30 minutes after the collision, at 1 p.m. New Zealand time on Saturday, the crew activated an emergency beacon and declared a full mayday. New Zealand crew member Terry Hetherington recounted spending the subsequent hours bailing water in a desperate attempt to save the yacht. French crew member Martin Jaffre battled to slow the incoming water, using expansion foam and even swimming below the boat to inspect the damaged hull, which had multiple gashes and a cracked fiberglass structure, rendering the steering inoperable.

Despite their efforts to keep the engine from clogging and to manually bail water, the situation deteriorated. Late on Saturday night, under a full moon and in calm seas, the crew made the difficult decision to abandon the Tai Tam and transfer to a life raft. In the early hours of Sunday morning, fearing the sinking yacht might drag them down, they cut the tether. Soon after, the Tai Tam slipped beneath the waves, a moment captured in dramatic drone video released by the New Zealand military. The Royal New Zealand Air Force had dispatched a P-8A Poseidon patrol plane to establish radio communications and coordinate the successful rescue.

Key Takeaways

  • A sperm whale collision severely damaged and ultimately sank the 52-foot yacht Tai Tam in the remote South Pacific.
  • Four international sailors endured an 18-hour survival ordeal, including bailing water and abandoning ship for a life raft.
  • The Royal New Zealand Air Force coordinated a successful rescue operation after the crew activated an emergency beacon.

Why It Matters

This incident highlights the inherent dangers and unpredictable challenges of sailing in remote ocean environments. The swift and coordinated response by the Royal New Zealand Air Force underscores the critical role of maritime search and rescue services in saving lives under extreme circumstances. The crew's resilience and quick thinking, from activating their emergency beacon to their efforts to mitigate damage and safely abandon ship, were crucial to their survival in a situation where human activity intersects with the powerful and often unseen forces of marine wildlife.
